extracted.intended_audience: program evaluators, educational researchers, and MER (Mathematics Education Reform) project stakeholders
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and empirical criteria for evaluating a professional mathematics-education network (MER), including case-study design, survey instrument development, sampling decisions, outreach effectiveness metrics, and interpretation caveats. Focuses on methods and evaluative dimensions used to assess MER's reach, communications, and impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Case selection: purposive best-case sampling with representation
rubrics_metrics.description: Selected institutions where evaluators expected to find a best-case-scenario of active educational agendas; chosen to provide both geographic and programmatic representation (Mid-Atlantic, East Coast, Southwest, West Coast).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid purely random selection if it would prevent learning about network dynamics; select cases that show active agendas, and ensure geographic and programmatic spread. One evaluator spent approximately one week at each department.

rubrics_metrics.name: Case study balance: pre-ordinate checklist plus responsive approach
rubrics_metrics.description: Combine an a priori checklist of documents/activities with a flexible, responsive approach during site visits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A priori items included interviewing department chair, meeting graduate students, talking with pro-/neutral-/anti-MER participants, and attending at least one 'reformed' mathematics class. Carry out agenda items in ways appropriate to each department and allow site-salient themes to guide activities to maintain balance between pre-ordinate and responsive case study methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Survey population choice: census of participants rather than sampling
rubrics_metrics.description: Chose to survey the entire target population (730 past and current MER participants) instead of sampling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When subpopulation membership cannot be identified (precluding stratification), surveying the whole population can maximize inclusion of small subgroups (e.g., K-12 teachers, math educators) and 'saturate' the sample to improve absolute numbers from underrepresented groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stratification limitation and sampling constraint
rubrics_metrics.description: Unable to stratify or use multi-stage sampling due to lack of descriptive information identifying individuals' professional-community affiliation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledge when data do not permit probabilistic sampling; explain the prohibition and the consequences for representativeness and analytic options.

rubrics_metrics.name: Over-sampling strategy for small subgroups when identities unknown
rubrics_metrics.description: Because small subgroups (K-12, math educators) could not be identified, the evaluators mailed all three questionnaires to uncertain recipients to maximize chances of including these groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When you cannot oversample specific groups by selection, use whole-population mailings or other saturation techniques to increase response counts from small subpopulations; document the trade-offs (e.g., inability to compute precise subgroup response rates).

rubrics_metrics.name: Instrument development: stakeholder collaboration and language learning
rubrics_metrics.description: Instrument development used active collaboration with co-directors, advisory committee, and task force to 'learn the language' of participants and craft mutually understandable questions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Iteratively solicit feedback from program leadership and stakeholders on drafts; aim to use terms and framings that participants recognize to improve relevance and response quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of existing instruments and literature to inform survey design
rubrics_metrics.description: A literature search and review of prior MER survey (1992 Berger survey) and other instruments (e.g., Faculty at Work) provided insight for question development.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leverage validated or relevant prior instruments and published literature to inform question content and structure; combine sources and stakeholder feedback as the basis for initial survey drafts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pilot testing multiple times in relevant settings
rubrics_metrics.description: Pilot tested instruments three times at relevant MER meetings/workshops (Baton Rouge workshop, Dec 1994 Task Force meeting, Jan 1995 Advisory Committee meeting).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conduct pilots in authentic settings with representative stakeholders; use results to iterate and decide final approach. Multiple pilots improve both data quality and response rates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Questionnaire format to reduce skipping complexity
rubrics_metrics.description: Created three separate questionnaires (one per professional community) to eliminate complicated skipping patterns and encourage completion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When respondents belong to distinct professional communities, provide separate, clearly labeled forms to simplify instructions and reduce respondent burden, even at added mailing cost.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cover letter instructions and encouragement of partial returns
rubrics_metrics.description: Cover letter explained forms, asked respondents to complete only the appropriate form, estimated 20-25 minute completion time, and encouraged returning even partially completed surveys (at minimum demographics and closed-ended questions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use clear cover-letter language to direct respondents to the correct form, set realistic time expectations, and explicitly permit/encourage partial completion to improve usable response yield and capture essential data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of small incentives and follow-up reminders to boost response
rubrics_metrics.description: Consultation suggested a $2 MER coupon for a banquet as an incentive; a follow-up postcard was mailed about two weeks after initial mailing to remind participants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider modest incentives targeted to the population and timely follow-up reminders (postcards/emails) as strategies to improve response rates; document rationales and limitations (e.g., incentive appeal may be limited to supportive respondents).

rubrics_metrics.name: Response rate calculation and subgroup-rate caveats
rubrics_metrics.description: Reported a 32% overall usable response rate (230 usable questionnaires) and noted inability to calculate precise subgroup response rates due to sending multiple forms to ambiguous recipients.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When survey administration choices prevent exact subgroup denominators, transparently report overall rates and explain why subgroup rates are approximate or uncomputable; discuss likely direction of bias (e.g., mathematician response rate appears higher).

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge self-selection and limits to generalizability
rubrics_metrics.description: Respondents were self-selected (volunteers), making it impossible to accurately generalize to the target population; estimates may under- or overstate impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly state self-selection bias, avoid overgeneralization, and frame interpretations as contingent on sampled/respondent characteristics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demographic representativeness comparison to national benchmarks
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare respondent demographics (race/ethnicity, gender, rank, age, tenure, affiliations) to national statistics to assess representativeness and discuss implications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use external benchmarks (e.g., national faculty counts) to contextualize sample composition (e.g., MER attracts more women and more tenured/older faculty than national averages) and interpret program reach and inclusiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation thematic organizer for program effectiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Separated MER's functions into themes for evaluation: (1) extent MER reaches target audience of research mathematicians; (2) effectiveness of communication activities; (3) breadth and depth of educational initiatives; (4) impact of workshops; (5) extent MER meets needs of mathematicians and K-12 educators; (6) systemic effects of activities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure findings around explicit, pre-specified thematic dimensions to organize evidence and interpretation about program effectiveness across multiple functional areas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment of communication/ outreach channels
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate varied outreach avenues (word of mouth, newsletters, mailings, Joint Societies Meetings, workshops, CBMS volumes) by asking how respondents learned about MER and which channels are useful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure both recruitment effectiveness (which channels attract new members) and retention/information utility (which channels inform existing members); analyze by subgroup to detect differential channel effectiveness (e.g., word of mouth most effective overall).

rubrics_metrics.name: Newsletter utility as a metric (update vs recruit)
rubrics_metrics.description: Newsletter found useful to existing participants (around 75-80% say helpful) but ineffective for recruiting new members (very few learned of MER from the newsletter).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between communications that maintain member engagement and those that recruit new members; evaluate newsletter sections (feature articles, essays, basic activities, MSEB info) for relative value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conference special sessions as outreach and engagement metric
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess special sessions by attendance, audience engagement (discussions, standing-room-only), pedagogical modeling, and ability to spark debate; note session topics and audience reactions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use session attendance and qualitative indicators (lively discussion, standing-room-only) as proxies for interest and influence; examine whether sessions model good pedagogy and address controversial issues effectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication (CBMS volumes) awareness and usefulness metric
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure awareness, reading rates, and perceived usefulness of CBMS Issues in Mathematics Education volumes; found limited readership and mixed usefulness ratings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Track readership and utility of edited volumes as part of outreach evaluation; low readership suggests limited effectiveness as a mass communication strategy for the target audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analysis of inclusiveness vs mission-focused specialization
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider trade-offs between being a selective, research-mathematician-focused organization and expanding openness to increase inclusiveness; some respondents perceived MER as elitist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether widening access would further systemic reform goals without alienating core target groups; use participant feedback to weigh decisions about openness, recruitment, and perceived elitism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretive caution about latent scope of impact
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that MER may impact a larger group than workshop attendees and that numerical estimates of impact may be underestimates; make interpretations ultimately for stakeholders (co-directors, funders).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State limitations of measurement and the potential for broader indirect effects; present alternative interpretations and leave final judgment to program leadership and funders.
